newsitem.title: UK: North Sea crude gains as Nigerian clears, arbs open.
newsitem.headline: North Sea crude gains as Nigerian clears, arbs open.

text.p: North Sea crudes were firmer on Friday, gaining strength from signs of early May cargoes leaving northwest Europe for refineries in the Mediterranean, United States and Far East, traders said.
June Brent rallied 30 cents to $17.99 a barrel by 1830 GMT and intermonth spreads were also stronger, May/June trading as high as -21 cents after Thursday's deals at -30 and -34 cents.
"It's difficult to get to grips with this market. Lots of deals are being done privately, but the arbitrages should be workable and West Africa has cleared out pretty well," said a trader.

A flurry of demand this week from Asian refiners for West African crudes encouraged North Sea sellers to measure up arbitrage opportunities to the U.S. Gulf in the hope of finding some requirements left uncovered.
Traders also cited talk of early May Oseberg going to the Far East and shipping brokers reports of China's Sinochem fixing a VLCC to take Brent to the Mediterranean.

Brent CFDs rallied strongly, next week's dates gaining about 12 cents to June Brent -50/-46 cents amid signs of a pick up in demand for the benchmark grade. Shell kept four of the cargoes turning wet on Friday. The fifth was clocked to Texaco.
But the tighter West African market was the main factor behind the improving sentiment, dealers said.
Japanese, South Korean and Chinese buyers have all been active this week, picking up at least seven million barrels of Nigerian and Angolan crudes loading in May.
Traders said spot differentials were still firming as a result, Bonny Light trading at Dated Brent +35/+36 cents on Thursday and Qua Iboe at Dated Brent +31 cents.
In the Mediterranean, Algerian price talks continued with the state oil company Sonatrach "targeting something in the (Dated Brent plus) 50s for Saharan Blend," said a lifter.
Sellers of Russian Urals were trying to stick to current levels of about Dated Brent -$1.15 but buyers were seeking lower prices, expecting cheaper May alternatives to exert pressure.
